definition: Roblox VFX (particle emitters, beams, trails) are anchored to a moving target via a lightweight Attachment instance parented under the relevant rig part, so the effect translates and rotates rigidly with whatever the attachment is parented to; separately, because firing a ParticleEmitter from a client-side LocalScript is only visible to that one client, any effect other players must see is triggered on the server (directly, or via a RemoteEvent the client fires to request it) so it replicates to everyone.
purpose: Solve two separate problems the same demonstrated workflow addresses together: getting a VFX to sit at the correct moving/rotating point in space (the attachment's job), and making sure every player who should see the effect actually does (the server-authority job).
visible_effect: A particle/beam effect tracks a body part's motion exactly, including rotation, because it is parented to an attachment on that part; the same effect is visible identically to every client because it was fired from the server rather than a LocalScript.
psychological_or_gameplay_effect: An effect only the local player can see reads as a bug or desync to everyone else in a multiplayer game — a shot with a visible muzzle flash on the shooter's own screen only breaks the read of "something happened" for every other player watching.
physical_interpretation: Not applicable — a networking/authority concern layered on top of a simple parenting mechanism, not a motion-physics one.
use_cases: any VFX that must move and rotate with a specific rig part (a muzzle flash on a gun barrel, a hand glow, a weapon trail)
any VFX that other players in a multiplayer session are expected to see, not only the player who triggered it
non_use_cases: a VFX anchored to a runtime-computed world point rather than a declared part (an impact placed via raycast hit position) — a different technique from the same video, see raycast_derived_impact_vfx_placement
a purely local, cosmetic effect nobody else needs to see (e.g. a first-person-only UI flourish), where server authority would be unnecessary overhead
interactions: animation_marker_triggered_vfx_emit (this same video) — the attachment says WHERE the effect appears; the marker says WHEN it fires. The video uses both together (attachment inside the arm, triggered at the animation's "shoot" marker)

raycast_derived_impact_vfx_placement (this same video) — the direct counterexample: an impact effect anchors to a computed hit point instead of a declared attachment, because its position is not known until the shot resolves
cadence_representation: The anchoring half is already exactly what VFXSpec models: the `anchor` field (`{itemId, partId}`) parents the compiled `kind:'vfx'` emitter item to a declared part, the same relationship this video builds by hand with an Attachment instance. The server/client authority half has no Cadence analogue at all: Cadence authors a single project's keyframed data and exports it (`vfx_export_luau`, `export_to_studio`); it does not generate or reason about networking (a RemoteEvent, which script runs where), so whether an exported effect ends up client-local or server-authoritative is entirely a fact about what the exporting user does with the result, not something Cadence's tools check or enforce.
control_surface: `compile_effect`'s `anchor` field for the parenting half. Nothing in the MCP surface inspects or asserts where a script runs, since Cadence does not author scripts.
detection_and_measurement_methods: not measurable in this build — this is a fact about a generated script's runtime network behavior, and `ai/motion.js` measures keyframed motion inside one project, never where a script executes or who a replicated event reaches.
generation_or_modification_methods: `compile_effect`'s `anchor` parameter sets the parent part; nothing generates the surrounding Roblox script (the RemoteEvent wiring, the server-side emit call) that the video's networking half is actually about.
failure_modes: firing the effect from a LocalScript only, so only the triggering player ever sees it — reads as a desync or missing effect to everyone else
anchoring to the wrong part (or no attachment at all), so the effect floats at the part's origin instead of tracking the intended point
roblox_considerations: Attachment is a real Instance type and the standard way to give an emitter/beam a moving anchor point. ParticleEmitter/Beam effects fired with `:Emit()` from a LocalScript are LOCAL-ONLY to that client — anything meant to be seen by more than the triggering player must run on the server, directly or via a RemoteEvent the client uses to request it. This is a foundational Roblox networking fact independent of any authoring tool.
performance_implications: None specifically measured in the video; it does mention cleaning up cloned effect instances a couple of seconds after use as good hygiene, not as a measured budget.
examples: "Attachments are basically points in your model that tell the effect where to appear... your VFX will move and rotate with whatever they're attached to" (video @ 00:49–00:57), visually confirmed by this session's own frame at t≈00:39–00:49 showing a small magenta attachment gizmo appear on a plain wall surface in the Studio viewport
"If you play effects locally, only you will see them. So, instead, we use the server to handle the VFX. That way, every player can see them" (video @ 02:27–02:39)

"Right here, I'm creating an attachment inside the arm, which is where the VFX will be played. The effects are cloned from replicated storage" (video @ 03:44–03:54), corroborated by a code-editor frame at t≈03:41 consistent with an Attachment being created and parented to an arm part
evidence_status: video: https://youtu.be/TkNZETIu0CM @ 00:49–00:57, 02:27–02:39, 03:44–03:54 — Develuper demonstrates attachment-based anchoring and explicitly states the client/server visibility distinction; experimental until validated
